subsection: 6. Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions

notes.h: The process: urbanisation and rural-to-urban migration
notes.b: Urbanisation is the growing share of people living in towns; urban growth is the rise in the number of people living in towns.
points: Rural-to-urban migration is the main driver of urbanisation in developing countries; natural increase in the cities is the other driver.
Over half the world's people have lived in urban areas since about 2007 (UN).
About 68% of the world's people are expected to be urban by 2050 (UN, 2018 projection).
The fastest urban growth is now in Asia and Africa, where megacities are forming.
Lack of jobs and low farm incomes.
Mechanisation of farming, which reduces the labour needed on the land.
Small, subdivided holdings that cannot support a family.
Poor services, including schools, hospitals, broadband and transport.
Drought, famine and land degradation in the developing world.
Isolation and lack of social life.
Jobs in industry and services.
Higher wages.
Third-level education.
Better health care and services.
Entertainment and the 'bright lights' of the city.
Existing family networks, which create chain migration.
Counter-urbanisation is people moving out of cities to towns and the countryside, found in developed countries.
Remote working since COVID-19 lets people live outside cities while working in them.

notes.h: Ireland: from a rural to an urban country
notes.b: Ireland was a rural country until the later 20th century, and its population then concentrated in cities.
points: Census 1971 was the first census in which more people lived in towns than in rural areas.
Census 2016: about 63% of the population was urban.
Flight from the land: farming mechanised and small farms became unviable, so people moved to cities.
Industrial and service jobs concentrated in Dublin and the cities.

notes.b: Growth is concentrated in Dublin, with the commuter counties and the regional cities also growing.
points: Census 2022: the State had about 5.15 million people.

Co. Dublin had about 1.46 million; Dublin city and suburbs had about 1.26 million; the Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) had about 2.1 million, about 40% of the State's population.
Dublin is the primate city, a city much larger than any other in its country.
Commuter towns include Navan, Drogheda, Naas and Newbridge.
Regional cities (city and suburbs): Cork about 220,000; Limerick about 100,000; Galway city about 85,000; Waterford about 60,000.
Dublin's earlier planned growth created the new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown under the Myles Wright plan of 1967.

notes.h: Impacts on the receiver region: Dublin
points: A large labour pool attracts multinationals and service firms.
Economies of scale support transport, universities and hospitals.
A rich cultural life.
Housing shortages, high rents and prices, and homelessness.
Urban sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow.
Long commutes and traffic congestion.
Pressure on water supply and other services.
High-rise and infill development pressure.

notes.h: Impacts on the donor region: the West and North-West
notes.b: Rural decline in Ireland is now local, in remote parishes and townlands, rather than county-wide.
points: Census 2022: the population of every county grew between 2016 and 2022, so decline is within counties rather than whole counties.
Leitrim had about 155,000 people in 1841 and about 35,000 in Census 2022, the least populous county.
Mayo had about 138,000 people and about 25 people per km² in Census 2022; Co. Dublin had about 1,600 per km².
An ageing population and higher dependency ratios.
Fewer young adults and lower birth rates.
Closure of schools, post offices, Garda stations, shops and pubs, and derelict houses.
Loss of community and sporting clubs, with GAA teams amalgamating, and farms with no successor.
Cultural loss, including the decline of the Gaeltacht.
Positive effects: less pressure on land, remittances and returning migrants, and some farm consolidation.
The National Spatial Strategy (2002) set out gateways and hubs to spread growth.
The decentralisation programme, announced in 2003, moves public service jobs out of Dublin.
The Western Development Commission has been a statutory body since 1999.
CLÁR, a programme of investment in depopulated rural areas, was launched in 2001.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, founded in 1980, creates jobs in the Gaeltacht.

The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), published in February 2018, plans for about 1 million more people by 2040, with about half of growth in the five cities (Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford) and their suburbs, and with the four cities other than Dublin growing faster than Dublin.
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme and rural broadband with remote working hubs support rural areas.
Limitation: rural areas and regional cities still depend on the jobs and services that drew people to Dublin.
Italy: after the Second World War, people moved from the Mezzogiorno to the industrial cities of the north, Turin and Milan, and abroad to Germany, Switzerland and Belgium.
The Mezzogiorno has about 20 million people (2020s), about one-third of Italy's population.
Depopulating southern villages responded with €1 house schemes, such as Sambuca di Sicilia.
France: Paris dominates the country; Jean-François Gravier's Paris et le désert français (1947) described the regions outside Paris as a French desert.
Île-de-France has about 12 million people (2020s), about 18% of France's population.

notes.b: Migration from poor rural states to the big cities fills slums and sends remittances back to the villages.
points: Migrants come from poorer rural states, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, to Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.
Push factors: small holdings, debt, landlessness and drought.
Pull factors: jobs in construction, factories and the informal sector.
Census 2011: about 31% of Indians were urban, up from about 17% in 1951; about 833 million people (about 69%) were rural.
Census 2011 urban agglomerations: Greater Mumbai about 18.4 million; Delhi about 16.3 million; Kolkata about 14.1 million.
Bihar is India's densest state, at about 1,100 per km².
About 65 million people lived in slums.

Dharavi, Mumbai, is one of Asia's largest slums, about 2 km² near the city centre, with hundreds of thousands of residents and many small industries such as recycling, leather, pottery and garments. Kolkata's slums are called bustees.
Receiver impacts: pressure on water, sanitation and transport; informal work; and a large supply of cheap labour.
Donor impacts: male out-migration leaves women, children and the old to farm; remittances fund houses, education and farm inputs; working-age labour is lost.
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances, mostly from international migrants, so the figure does not measure rural-to-urban flows directly.
In the March 2020 COVID-19 lockdown, millions of migrant workers walked or travelled home from the cities.

notes.b: Brazil's migration runs from the drought-prone North-East to the south-east, and Brazil is now highly urbanised.
points: Migrants from the sertão, the drought-prone semi-arid interior of the North-East (nordestinos), moved to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro; some also helped build Brasília, the capital from 1960.
Census 2022: Brazil had about 203 million people, about 87% of them urban (2020s).
São Paulo city had about 11.5 million people (Census 2022), and over 20 million in its metropolitan region; it is Brazil's largest city and industrial centre.
Favelas on hillsides and at the urban edge; Rocinha in Rio de Janeiro is one of Brazil's largest.
Informal work is common in the favelas, and some favelas have crime and gang violence.
The North-East, the donor region, loses young people.
The hukou (household registration) system, introduced in 1958, ties public services to a person's registered home.
Nearly 300 million rural migrant workers (2023), many of them in coastal cities such as Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Shanghai.
Shenzhen grew from a small town to a city of over 17 million after becoming China's first Special Economic Zone in 1980.
China's urban share passed 50% in 2011.
Rural villages are left with 'left-behind' children and elderly people.
Migrants lack full access to urban schools, health care and housing.
Hukou reform is gradual.

notes.h: Contrasting impacts: developed and developing regions
notes.b: The scale, speed and capacity of cities differ between the two kinds of region, so the impacts differ.
points: In developed regions migration is slower, and cities can largely absorb it with planned housing and services.
In developed regions the donor problem is ageing rural decline.
In developing regions migration is fast and very large; cities cannot provide housing, jobs or services, so slums and the informal sector grow.
In developing regions donor villages depend on remittances and lose working-age men.
Urban growth in developing cities comes from both migration and high natural increase among young migrants.

keyTerms.definition: The growing share of a country's population living in towns and cities.
The movement of people out of cities to towns and the countryside.
Migration in which people move to places where family or community members have already settled.
A city much larger than any other city in its country.
Money sent home by migrants to their families.
The Chinese household registration system that ties public services to a person's registered home, introduced in 1958.
An informal settlement on hillsides or at the urban edge in Brazil.
The name for a slum in Kolkata.
The poorer south of Italy, with about 20 million people.

factCards.term: Rural-to-urban migration: push factors from rural areas
factCards.definition: Lack of jobs and low farm incomes; mechanisation of farming; small, subdivided holdings; poor services (schools, hospitals, broadband, transport); drought, famine and land degradation in the developing world; isolation and lack of social life.

factCards.term: Rural-to-urban migration: pull factors to cities
factCards.definition: Jobs in industry and services; higher wages; third-level education; better health care and services; entertainment and the bright lights of the city; family already there, creating chain migration.

factCards.term: Ireland's urbanisation: when it happened and why
factCards.definition: Census 1971 was the first with more people in towns than rural areas; about 63% were urban by 2016. Farming mechanised and small farms became unviable, while industrial and service jobs concentrated in Dublin and the other cities.

factCards.term: Growth in Irish cities: Census 2022 figures
factCards.definition: Dublin city and suburbs about 1.26 million; Co. Dublin about 1.46 million; Greater Dublin Area about 2.1 million (about 40% of the State). Cork about 220,000; Limerick about 100,000; Galway city about 85,000; Waterford about 60,000.

factCards.term: Dublin as a receiver region: positive impacts
factCards.definition: A large labour pool attracts multinationals and service firms; economies of scale support transport, universities and hospitals; a rich cultural life.

factCards.term: Dublin as a receiver region: negative impacts
factCards.definition: Housing shortages, high rents and prices, and homelessness; sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow and commuter towns such as Navan, Drogheda, Naas and Newbridge; long commutes and congestion; pressure on water supply and services.

factCards.term: The West and North-West as a donor region: negative impacts
factCards.definition: An ageing population and higher dependency ratios; fewer young adults and births; closed schools, post offices, Garda stations, shops and pubs; derelict houses; GAA teams amalgamating; farms with no successor; Gaeltacht decline.

factCards.term: Rural decline in Ireland: Leitrim, Mayo and Census 2022
factCards.definition: Leitrim fell from about 155,000 people (1841) to about 35,000 (2022), the least populous county; Mayo has about 25 people per km², against about 1,600 in Co. Dublin. Every county grew from 2016 to 2022, so decline is now local, in remote areas.

factCards.term: Irish responses to rural decline: name six
factCards.definition: National Spatial Strategy (2002): gateways and hubs; Western Development Commission (from 1999); CLÁR (2001) for depopulated rural areas; decentralisation of public service jobs (2003); Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980); rural broadband and remote working hubs.

factCards.term: National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040): its aims
factCards.definition: Published February 2018: plans for about 1 million more people by 2040, with about half of the growth in the five cities (Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway, Waterford) and their suburbs, and the four cities other than Dublin growing faster than Dublin.

factCards.term: Italy and France: European examples of rural-to-urban migration
factCards.definition: Italy: post-war migration from the Mezzogiorno to Turin and Milan; €1 house schemes in depopulating villages such as Sambuca di Sicilia. France: Gravier's Paris et le désert français (1947); Île-de-France holds about 18% of France's people.

factCards.term: India: why people migrate from rural to urban areas
factCards.definition: Migrants leave poorer rural states, Bihar (the densest, about 1,100 per km²) and Uttar Pradesh, for Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata, pushed by small holdings, debt, landlessness and drought, and pulled by jobs in construction, factories and the informal sector.

factCards.term: India: impacts on the receiver cities
factCards.definition: About 65 million people lived in slums (2011): Dharavi, Mumbai, about 2 km² near the centre, with small industries (recycling, leather, pottery, garments); bustees in Kolkata. Water, sanitation and transport are strained, but cities gain cheap labour.

factCards.term: India: impacts on the donor villages
factCards.definition: Male out-migration leaves women, children and the old to farm; remittances fund houses, education and farm inputs; working-age labour is lost. In the March 2020 COVID-19 lockdown, millions of migrant workers walked or travelled home.

factCards.term: Brazil: migration from the North-East, from where to where
factCards.definition: Nordestinos left the sertão, the drought-prone semi-arid interior of the North-East, for São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, and some helped build Brasília (capital from 1960). Brazil is now about 87% urban (2020s).

factCards.term: Brazil: impacts on the cities and on the North-East
factCards.definition: São Paulo city reached about 11.5 million (Census 2022), over 20 million in its metropolitan region; favelas grew on hillsides and at the urban edge, such as Rocinha in Rio; informal work, and gang crime in some favelas; the North-East loses young people.

factCards.term: China: rural migrant workers and the hukou system
factCards.definition: Nearly 300 million rural migrant workers (2023), many in coastal cities such as Shenzhen, which grew to over 17 million after becoming the first Special Economic Zone (1980). Under hukou (1958) they lack full urban services; children and elderly are left behind.

factCards.term: Rural-to-urban migration: developed and developing regions contrasted
factCards.definition: Developed: slower migration, absorbed by planned housing and services; the donor problem is ageing rural decline. Developing: fast, huge migration; cities lack housing, jobs and services, so slums and informal work grow; villages rely on remittances.

questions.prompt: Examine the contrasting impacts of rural-to-urban migration on donor and receiver regions in the developed and developing world.
questions.model: Ireland shows the developed-world pattern. Dublin is the receiver: its labour pool attracts multinationals and services, but housing shortages, high rents, urban sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow and long commutes follow. The Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State. The donor, the West and North-West, suffers an ageing population, fewer young adults, closure of schools, post offices and shops, derelict houses and the loss of community clubs, and farms with no successor. Responses include the National Spatial Strategy (2002), the National Planning Framework (2018), decentralisation and CLÁR. India shows the developing-world pattern. Migrants from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh move to Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata because of small holdings, debt and drought, and to jobs in construction, factories and the informal sector. Greater Mumbai had about 18.4 million people in Census 2011. The receivers face slums, such as Dharavi, pressure on water, sanitation and transport, and informal work, but gain cheap labour. The donor villages lose working-age men, leaving women, children and the old to farm, while remittances fund houses, education and farm inputs. The contrast: in developed countries migration is slower and cities can absorb it with planned housing and services, and the donor problem is ageing rural decline; in developing countries migration is fast and very large, cities cannot provide housing, jobs or services, and donor villages depend on remittances and lose their working-age men.

questions.prompt: (i) State two reasons why people migrate from rural to urban areas. (ii) Describe and explain the effect of this migration on the urban areas people migrate to. (iii) Describe and explain the effect on the rural areas they leave.
questions.model: (i) People migrate from rural to urban areas because of push factors such as a lack of jobs and low farm incomes, and because of pull factors such as jobs in industry and services and higher wages. (ii) In Dublin, the receiver city, the large labour pool attracts multinationals and services, and economies of scale support transport, universities and hospitals. However, demand for housing outstrips supply, which raises rents and prices and causes homelessness. Urban sprawl extends into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow, and long commutes cause traffic congestion and put pressure on water supply and services. (iii) In the West and North-West, the donor region, young adults leave, so the population ages, the dependency ratio rises and birth rates fall. Closures of schools, post offices, Garda stations and shops follow, and derelict houses appear. Local clubs amalgamate and farms have no successor, and the decline of the Gaeltacht threatens culture. Some effects are positive: there is less pressure on land, and remittances and returning migrants bring money and skills. Census 2022 showed that every county grew between 2016 and 2022, so decline is now local, in remote parishes and townlands.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of rural-to-urban migration in one developing country you have studied.
questions.model: Brazil shows the impact of rural-to-urban migration in a developing country. Migrants from the sertão, the drought-prone semi-arid interior of the North-East (nordestinos), move south-east to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro in search of jobs and better living conditions. The receiver cities struggle to house them. São Paulo city had about 11.5 million people in Census 2022, and over 20 million in its metropolitan region, and it is Brazil's largest city and industrial centre. Migrants settle in favelas on hillsides and at the urban edge, such as Rocinha in Rio de Janeiro, one of Brazil's largest. Work there is often informal, and some favelas have crime and gang violence. The donor region, the North-East, loses young people, which reduces its working-age population and its capacity to develop. Brazil is now about 87% urban, so the flow that once drew people from the interior has been absorbed into a highly urbanised country. Evaluation: migration has supplied labour to industry and built the urban economy, but it has also created informal settlements and social problems that cities have struggled to manage.
